metadata.title: GitHub Actions — Security and CI/CD Best Practices

entries.description: Structure a DevSecOps CI/CD pipeline with: (1) test job (lint + pytest), (2) sast job (Semgrep + CodeQL), (3) dependency-scan job (Gitleaks + OWASP Dependency-Check + Safety), (4) docker-build job with Trivy scan, (5) push-image job (main branch only, OIDC auth to ECR). Set global permissions: contents: read. Grant additional permissions per job only as needed.
decision_rules: Set global permissions: contents: read at workflow level — override per job for elevated needs
Gate docker-build on test and sast completion via needs: [test, sast]
Restrict push-image to main branch only via if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
tradeoffs: More pipeline stages add latency — parallelize independent jobs (test, sast, dependency-scan) to reduce wall-clock time
anti_patterns: Setting permissions: write-all at workflow level — grant minimum permissions per job
Pushing images before security scans pass
aws_alignment: Use OIDC (id-token: write permission) for AWS authentication — no long-lived access keys

entries.description: Use ${{ secrets.NAME }} syntax for all sensitive values. Never echo or print secrets. Use OIDC (id-token: write) for AWS/GCP authentication instead of long-lived access key pairs. Never hardcode credentials (e.g. AWS_ACCESS_KEY: AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE) directly in workflow YAML.
decision_rules: Reference all secrets via ${{ secrets.NAME }} — never inline credentials
Use OIDC role assumption (aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials with role-to-assume) instead of static AWS keys
Rotate any accidentally exposed secret immediately
tradeoffs: OIDC setup requires creating an IAM OIDC provider and IAM role with trust policy — one-time setup cost
anti_patterns: Hardcoding AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID or any token directly in workflow YAML
Using echo or run: echo ${{ secrets.SECRET }} — GitHub may mask but this is risky
Storing long-lived AWS access keys as GitHub Secrets
aws_alignment: Configure AWS IAM OIDC provider for github.com to enable keyless AWS authentication from GitHub Actions

entries.description: Configure .github/dependabot.yml with update schedules for pip, docker, and github-actions ecosystems. Set interval: weekly, open-pull-requests-limit: 5, and labels for triage. Dependabot automatically creates PRs when new versions are available.
decision_rules: Enable Dependabot for all three ecosystems: pip (Python deps), docker (base images), github-actions (action versions)
Set open-pull-requests-limit to prevent too many PRs from overwhelming the team
tradeoffs: Dependabot PRs require review — can generate noise if not triaged promptly
Auto-merge should only be enabled for patch-level updates with passing tests
anti_patterns: Not pinning action versions (e.g. uses: actions/checkout@main) — makes Dependabot updates non-deterministic
Ignoring Dependabot PRs — allows dependency CVEs to accumulate

entries.concept: Complete FastAPI CI pipeline with PostgreSQL service and Trivy
entries.description: GitHub Actions CI for FastAPI: uses postgres:15 as a service container with health check (pg_isready, --health-interval 10s), runs pytest with DATABASE_URL pointing to the service container, builds Docker image with docker build, runs Trivy scan on the built image with severity CRITICAL and exit-code 1.
decision_rules: Use GitHub Actions service containers for integration testing with real databases
Set --health-cmd pg_isready with health-interval and health-retries to ensure PostgreSQL is ready before tests run
Run Trivy scan on the CI-built image before it can be promoted to any registry
tradeoffs: Service containers add startup time to the CI job — parallel job execution reduces overall pipeline time
anti_patterns: Mocking the database in integration tests — diverges from production behavior
Building and pushing Docker images without any vulnerability scan
